summary: This note covers the Nintendo Entertainment System (NES), the 8-bit console Nintendo released as the Famicom in Japan in 1983. It describes the console's design and development, the failed Atari distribution deal, its role in reviving the post-1983 crash market, its North American bundles, later hardware redesigns, and Nintendo's licensing controls and efforts against unlicensed games.
one_line: Overview of the Nintendo Entertainment System: its Famicom origins, North American launch and bundles, redesigns, and Nintendo's control over third-party developers.
key_facts: The Nintendo Entertainment System (NES) is an 8-bit home console developed and manufactured by Nintendo; it was released in Japan as the Family Computer (Famicom) on July 15, 1983.
The NES reached North America in 1985, Europe in 1986 and Australia in 1987; in South Korea it was the Hyundai Comboy, distributed by Hyundai Electronics (later SK Hynix).
The NES was succeeded by the Super Nintendo Entertainment System.

Nintendo negotiated with Atari to sell the Famicom as the Nintendo Advanced Video Gaming System, but the deal collapsed after Atari found Coleco illegally demonstrating its Coleco Adam with Donkey Kong at the June 1983 Summer CES and CEO Ray Kassar was fired the next month.

Masayuki Uemura designed the Famicom; Hiroshi Yamauchi rejected a planned 16-bit computer-like system with keyboard and floppy drive in favor of a cheaper cartridge console, since he felt keyboards and disks intimidated non-technophiles.
A Famicom test model was built in October 1982; because 65xx CPUs had not been sold in Japan, early games were written on an NEC PC-8001 computer-based system with no existing tools.
The NES relaunched a market damaged by the video game crash of 1983 by offering a single clearly defined platform instead of exaggerated packaging and inconsistent game versions.
The Deluxe Set sold for US$199.99 and included R.O.B., the NES Zapper, two controllers, and Gyromite and Duck Hunt.
The 1988 Action Set cost US$149.99, and the 1989 Power Set added a Power Pad and a triple Game Pak with Super Mario Bros, Duck Hunt and World Class Track Meet.
The 1992 Challenge Set sold for US$89.99 with the console, two controllers and Super Mario Bros. 3; the Basic Set included the Official Nintendo Player's Guide instead of a game.
In December 1993 the Famicom was redesigned as the AV Famicom (HVC-101) with composite video, top-loading cartridges and detachable controllers on 90 cm cables, versus 180 cm on NES controllers.
The new Famicom controllers lacked the microphone of the original second controller, so tricks in games like Disk System The Legend of Zelda and Raid on Bungeling Bay cannot be replicated.
Unlike Atari, Nintendo encouraged third-party developers strictly on its own terms, and some of its platform-control measures were later adopted by Sega, Sony and Microsoft.
Unlicensed developers bypassed the 10NES authentication chip with voltage-spike circuits or dongles, and Nintendo of America threatened retailers selling them with losing licensed titles.
